intro: You have heard the word Bible. Maybe you have seen one at home, in a library, or on a stand at a hotel. Maybe you have never opened one. In this unit you will find out what is inside. The Bible is not one book. It is a library of many books, and different groups keep different lists.

First you will learn how the library is built: its two big parts, its books, its chapters and verses, and the languages it was written in. You will learn to find any verse by its address. Then you will read the first five books, called the Torah, as one long story from the making of the world to the edge of a promised land.

This is a public school class. We study the Bible as literature and history. We say what the text says and how Jews and Christians read it. We never say it is true or false. By the end, you will be able to open a Bible, find your way, and explain its first big story to someone else.
bigQuestion: What is the Bible, and how does its first big story hold together?

title: What the Bible Is

chapters.title: A Library of Books
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do people call the Bible one book when it is really a whole library?

story.title: Four Bibles on One Table
story.kicker: A class finds the same sentence in four Bibles that do not look alike.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz puts four books on the table. One is huge and black with gold letters on the edge of the pages. One is small and blue and fits in a pocket. One has Hebrew letters on every page, and its front cover is where most books have their back cover. One is a paperback with a bright yellow spine and a cracked cover. "These are all Bibles," she says. "Or parts of one. Let's see if they agree."

She writes John 3:16 on the board. "Find it." The class opens the big black book. Near the back, they find a heading that says John, a big 3, and a tiny 16. There it is. The blue pocket Bible has it too, near the back. The words are almost the same, but one says believeth and one says believes.

Then Malik opens the Hebrew book. He looks and looks. There is no John in it at all. "That is a Tanakh," Ms. Ortiz says. "It is the Hebrew Bible. It has the books Jews read as scripture. John is a Christian book, so it is not here. But open the first page." Malik reads the first line in English: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. The big black Bible says the same thing on its first page.

Amara has the yellow paperback. She finds John 3:16 fast. But when she looks at the table of contents, she counts more books in the first part than the black Bible has. "This one is a Catholic Bible," says Ms. Ortiz. "It keeps a few books the others leave out." The class stares at the four books. Same sentence. Same first line. Different sizes, different lists, different words.

"So which one is the real Bible?" Amara asks. Ms. Ortiz smiles. "That is a question people have argued about for a very long time. In this class, we will learn what each one holds, who reads it, and why they do not look alike. Then you can ask better questions than I can."
story.think: The four books had the same first line but different lists of books. What do you think could make a book list change from one group to another?

lessons.title: A Library on One Shelf
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible is a collection of many smaller books, written over a long time by many people.
reading: The word *Bible* comes from a Greek word, biblia. It means "the books." That is a good name. The Bible is not one long story by one writer. It is a *library* of smaller books bound together. Some books are stories. Some are laws. Some are songs, letters or lists of names.

Open a Bible to the table of contents. You will see names like Genesis, Ruth, Psalms, Matthew and Romans. Each name is a separate book. Genesis is fifty chapters long. Some books, like Obadiah, are only one chapter. The books were written over many hundreds of years, in different places, by many different people.

Jews and Christians both call this library *scripture*. That word means holy writing. Jews believe the Hebrew Bible is scripture. Christians believe the Old Testament and the New Testament are scripture. In this class we do not decide who is right. We learn what the books say and how people read them.

words.d: a collection of books that Jews and Christians treat as scripture; the name means "the books"
a collection of many books kept together
writing that a religion treats as holy

look.title: One Cover, Many Books
look.text: Picture a shelf in a school library. On it sit a book of fairy tales, a book of rules for a game, a songbook, a stack of letters from a pen pal, and a family tree. Now picture someone gluing all of them into one cover and writing one title on the front.
look.prompt: How would you read that big book differently than you would read a single story? Which part would you look for first?

check.q: What does the word Bible mean?
check.why: Bible comes from the Greek word biblia, which means "the books."

check.q: Which sentence best describes the Bible?
choices: One long story by one writer
A library of many smaller books
check.why: The Bible is a collection of many books of different kinds, written by many people over a long time.

check.q: What does scripture mean?
choices: Writing a religion treats as holy
check.why: Scripture means holy writing. Jews and Christians both use this word for their Bibles.

lessons.title: Two Testaments, One Tanakh
lessons.mainIdea: Christian Bibles have an Old Testament and a New Testament; the Jewish Bible is called the Tanakh.
reading: A Christian Bible has two big parts. The first part is the *Old Testament*. It tells of creation, Abraham, Moses, kings and prophets. The second part is the *New Testament*. It tells of Jesus and his first followers. Christians believe the New Testament completes the Old. That is why they call the first part old.

Jews read the first part too, but they do not call it old. To them it is the whole Bible. They call it the *Tanakh*. That name is made from three Hebrew letters. T is for Torah, the teaching. N is for Nevi'im, the prophets. K is for Ketuvim, the writings. Put them together and you get Tanakh.

So the same books have two names. A Christian says Old Testament. A Jew says Tanakh or Hebrew Bible. Many scholars say Hebrew Bible in school, because that name does not pick a side. In this course we will use both names and say which one we mean.

words.d: the Christian name for the first part of the Bible, the books shared with the Hebrew Bible
the second part of the Christian Bible, about Jesus and his first followers
the Jewish name for the Hebrew Bible, from Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim

look.title: Two Names for One Set of Books
look.text: Reader A opens a book and says, "This is the Old Testament. It leads up to Jesus." Reader B opens the same book and says, "This is the Tanakh. It is our whole Bible." Both are reading Genesis, Isaiah and Psalms.
look.prompt: Why does the same set of books get a different name from each reader? Which name would you use in a school report, and why?

check.q: What are the two big parts of a Christian Bible called?
check.why: Christian Bibles are divided into the Old Testament and the New Testament.

check.q: What does the K in Tanakh stand for?
check.why: Tanakh comes from Torah, Nevi'im (prophets) and Ketuvim (writings).

check.q: Why do many scholars say Hebrew Bible instead of Old Testament?
choices: Because it is shorter to say
Because the books are written only in Hebrew
Because it is the oldest name
Because it does not pick one tradition's name
check.why: Hebrew Bible is a neutral name. It does not use the Christian word old or the Jewish word Tanakh.

lessons.title: Counting the Same Words
lessons.mainIdea: Protestant, Catholic and Jewish Bibles count their books differently, so 66, 73 and 24 can describe much of the same text.
reading: Ask three people how many books are in the Bible, and you may get three answers. Most *Protestant* Bibles have 66 books. *Catholic* Bibles have 73. The Hebrew Bible has 24. That sounds like a big fight. But part of it is just counting.

The Hebrew Bible counts Samuel as one book. Christian Bibles split it into 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel. The Hebrew Bible counts twelve short prophets as one book, called The Twelve. Christian Bibles count them as twelve books. Same words, different counting. That is how 24 books can hold the same text as 39.

Catholic Bibles also keep seven extra books, like Tobit, Judith and 1 and 2 Maccabees. Protestants call these books the *Apocrypha* and usually leave them out. Orthodox Christians keep even more. Each group has its own reasons. The lists differ, but every one of them agrees on Genesis, Psalms and Isaiah.

words.d: a Christian whose church grew out of the Reformation of the 1500s; Protestant Bibles have 66 books
a Christian in the church led by the pope in Rome; Catholic Bibles have 73 books
books like Tobit and Maccabees that Catholic Bibles include and most Protestant Bibles leave out

look.title: How Many Books?
look.cite: Standard book counts as printed in the JPS 1917 Tanakh, the King James Version and Catholic editions
look.prompt: The Hebrew Bible and the Protestant Old Testament hold the same text. How can one be 24 books and the other 39?

check.q: How many books are in most Protestant Bibles?
check.why: Protestant Bibles have 39 Old Testament books and 27 New Testament books, which makes 66.

check.q: Why does the Hebrew Bible count fewer books than the Protestant Old Testament?
choices: It counts some books as one that others split
It is written in a different alphabet
check.why: The Hebrew Bible counts Samuel, Kings and The Twelve as single books. The text is the same, only the counting differs.

check.q: Which Bible includes Tobit and 1 and 2 Maccabees?
check.why: Catholic Bibles keep these books. Protestants call them the Apocrypha and usually leave them out.

lessons.title: Chapters and Verses
lessons.mainIdea: Chapter and verse numbers were added long after the books were written, to help readers find the same place.
reading: Open any Bible and you see big numbers and tiny numbers. The big numbers are *chapters*. The tiny numbers are *verses*. A verse is usually one sentence or part of one. The numbers make it easy to find a spot. You can say Genesis 1:1 and a friend in another city can open to the same line.

The writers did not put those numbers in. Scrolls had no chapters. The chapter numbers most Bibles use came from a church leader in England named Stephen Langton, in the early 1200s. Jewish scribes had marked verse breaks long before that. The verse numbers we print today spread in the 1500s, after printing began.

So the numbers are a tool, not part of the text. Sometimes a chapter break lands in an odd place, right in the middle of a story. Careful readers know this. They read across the numbers and follow the words. Still, the numbers are a gift. Without them, finding one line in a library would take all day.

words.d: a big numbered section of a Bible book; the numbers were added in the 1200s
a small numbered part of a chapter, usually about one sentence long

look.title: How Big Is This Library?
look.cite: Chapter counts as printed in the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Psalms has 150 chapters, but each one is a song. Why might a book of songs need so many numbered parts?

check.q: What does the tiny number 16 in John 3:16 mark?
check.why: In John 3:16, the 3 is the chapter and the 16 is the verse.

check.q: Who is usually credited with the chapter numbers most Bibles use?
check.why: Stephen Langton, an English church leader, divided the books into chapters in the early 1200s.

check.q: Which sentence about chapter and verse numbers is true?
choices: They were added later as a finding tool
They are part of the holy text for all readers
They are only in the New Testament
check.why: Chapters and verses came centuries after the books were written. They help readers find the same place.

lessons.title: How to Find John 3:16
lessons.mainIdea: To find a verse, use the book name, then the chapter number, then the verse number.
reading: A Bible address has three parts. First comes the book name. Then the chapter. Then a colon and the verse. John 3:16 means the book of John, chapter 3, verse 16. Say it out loud: "John three sixteen." Now you can find it.

Step one: use the table of contents to find the page where John begins. It is in the New Testament, near the back. Step two: turn pages until you see the big number 3. Step three: run your finger down the small numbers until you reach 16. That is the verse.

Some addresses are longer. Genesis 1:1-5 means chapter 1, verses 1 through 5. Psalm 23 with no colon means the whole psalm. Once you know the pattern, you can find any line in the library. This one skill will help you all year.

words.d: the list at the front of a book that shows where each part begins
a Bible address made of book, chapter and verse, like John 3:16

look.title: The Verse the Class Found
look.text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
look.prompt: Christians treasure this verse. Find the three parts of its address: book, chapter and verse. Which part tells you it is in the New Testament?

check.q: In the reference Genesis 12:2, what does the 12 mean?
check.why: The number before the colon is the chapter. Genesis 12:2 is chapter 12, verse 2.

check.q: What does Psalm 23 with no colon mean?
choices: Only the first verse of Psalm 23
check.why: A book name and one number with no colon means the whole chapter.

check.q: What is the first step in finding a verse?
choices: Find the book name in the table of contents
Count the verses from page one
Look for the tiny number first
Open to the middle of the Bible
check.why: Start with the book, then the chapter, then the verse.

lessons.title: Kinds of Books Inside
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible's books come in kinds, such as law, story, poetry, prophecy and letters, and each kind is read a different way.
reading: Not every book in the Bible is the same kind of writing. Genesis is full of stories. Leviticus is mostly *law*, rules for how to live and worship. Psalms is a book of poems and songs. Isaiah is *prophecy*, speeches from someone who says he speaks for God. Romans is a *letter* to a church in Rome.

You read each kind differently. You do not read a songbook the way you read a rulebook. A story has characters and a plot. A letter has a greeting and a sender. A psalm repeats an idea in two ways, like an echo. Knowing the kind helps you know what to expect.

Christian Bibles group the Old Testament books as law, history, poetry and prophets. Jewish Bibles group them as Torah, Prophets and Writings. The New Testament has four Gospels, a history book called Acts, many letters, and one book of visions called Revelation. Learning the groups is like learning the sections of a library.

words.d: rules for how to live and worship; the Torah has many laws
a message that a prophet says comes from God, often spoken to kings and crowds
a message written to a person or group; many New Testament books are letters

look.title: Sort the Shelf
look.text: Four cards. Card 1: "Thou shalt not steal." Card 2: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." Card 3: "Paul, to the church in Corinth: grace to you." Card 4: "And Joseph dreamed a dream, and he told it to his brothers."
look.prompt: Which card is a law, which a song, which a letter, and which a story? What clue on each card told you?

check.q: Which book is mostly law?
check.why: Leviticus holds rules for living and worship. Psalms is songs, Ruth is a story and Romans is a letter.

check.q: What kind of writing is the book of Romans?
check.why: Romans is a letter written to the Christians in Rome.

check.q: How do Jewish Bibles group their books?
check.why: The Tanakh is grouped as Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings).

lessons.title: Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible was first written in three languages: Hebrew, a little Aramaic, and Greek.
reading: The Bible was not first written in English. Most of the Hebrew Bible was written in *Hebrew*. Hebrew reads from right to left. That is why a Tanakh opens from what looks like the back. Its letters look nothing like ours, but every one has a sound.

A few parts were written in *Aramaic*, a language close to Hebrew. Parts of the books of Daniel and Ezra are in Aramaic. Many scholars think Jesus spoke Aramaic every day. The New Testament, though, was written in *Greek*. Greek was the common language across much of the Roman world, so a letter in Greek could travel far.

Because of this, almost everyone who reads the Bible reads a *translation*. A translation moves words from one language to another. Every translator has to make choices. That is one big reason why the four Bibles on the class table did not use the same words.

words.d: the language of most of the Hebrew Bible; it reads from right to left
a language close to Hebrew, used in parts of Daniel and Ezra
the language of the New Testament, common across the Roman world
the same words moved from one language into another

look.title: Which Language, Which Books?
rows: Hebrew Bible books mainly in Hebrew
Books with sections in Aramaic (Daniel, Ezra)
look.cite: Language of the Hebrew Bible (JPS 1917) and the New Testament (KJV 1611); Aramaic sections in Daniel 2–7 and Ezra 4–7
look.prompt: Why might the New Testament writers choose Greek instead of Hebrew for their letters and Gospels?

check.q: In which language was most of the Hebrew Bible written?
check.why: Most of the Hebrew Bible is in Hebrew, with small parts in Aramaic.

check.q: Which books have parts written in Aramaic?
check.why: Parts of Daniel and Ezra are in Aramaic, a language close to Hebrew.

check.q: Why was the New Testament written in Greek?
choices: Greek was the language of Egypt
Greek was common across the Roman world
check.why: Greek was widely spoken in the Roman world, so writings in Greek could reach many readers.

lessons.title: The King James Bible of 1611
lessons.mainIdea: The King James Version, finished in 1611, became the most famous English Bible and shaped the English language.
reading: For a long time, most Bibles in Europe were in Latin. Only scholars could read them. In the 1500s, people began printing Bibles in the languages people spoke. Some were punished for it. William Tyndale printed an English New Testament in 1526 and was later put to death.

In 1604, King James of England ordered a new English Bible. About fifty scholars worked in teams for seven years. They used Tyndale's work and others. The result came out in 1611. People call it the *King James Version*, or KJV. It uses old words like thee, thou and believeth.

The King James Bible was read aloud in churches for hundreds of years. Its phrases slipped into everyday English. It is now in the *public domain*, so anyone may copy it for free. That is why this course quotes it often. Many Christians still love it, and many use newer Bibles too.

words.d: the English Bible finished in 1611 by scholars working for King James; also called the KJV
work that belongs to everyone and may be copied freely

look.title: The First Line, Two Ways
look.text: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
look.cite: Genesis 1:1, King James Version (1611); the Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917) prints the same English words
look.prompt: A Christian translation from 1611 and a Jewish translation from 1917 begin with the same sentence. What does that tell you about how carefully translators work?

check.q: In what year was the King James Version finished?
check.why: King James ordered it in 1604. The scholars finished it in 1611.

check.q: What does public domain mean?
check.why: A public domain work belongs to everyone. The KJV is old enough to be free for all.

check.q: Who printed an English New Testament in 1526?
check.why: William Tyndale printed his English New Testament in 1526, and the King James scholars used his work.

lessons.title: Newer Bibles, Same Books
lessons.mainIdea: Newer translations use modern words, and Jewish and Christian scholars each make their own.
reading: English keeps changing. Words like thee and thou dropped out of daily speech. So new translations keep coming. In 1917 the Jewish Publication Society made an English Tanakh for Jewish readers. In 1901 Christian scholars made the American Standard Version. Newer ones came in the 1970s and 1980s.

Some translators try to match each Hebrew or Greek word. Others try to say the meaning in easy modern sentences. Both goals are fair. This is why one Bible says believeth and another says believes. The meaning is the same. The style is different.

Look at the pocket Bible from the story. It is a newer *version*. A version is one translation among many. The Bible has now been translated, in whole or in part, into thousands of languages. Some people read it in Spanish, some in Swahili, some in sign language. Same library, many doors.

words.d: one translation of the Bible among many, like the KJV or the JPS 1917
a Jewish group that published an English Tanakh in 1917 and a newer one in 1985

look.title: The Same Verse, Three Translations
look.text: The King James Version (1611) says that God gave his "only begotten Son" and that whoever "believeth" in him will have "everlasting life." The American Standard Version (1901) keeps "only begotten Son" but says "eternal life." The World English Bible, a free modern translation, says God gave his "one and only Son," and that whoever "believes" in him will have "eternal life."
look.cite: John 3:16 in the King James Version (1611), the American Standard Version (1901) and the World English Bible (public domain)
look.prompt: The three translations use different words for the same Greek sentence. Does the meaning change? Which one would be easiest for a new reader?

check.q: Which translation did the Jewish Publication Society make in 1917?
check.why: The JPS Tanakh of 1917 is an English translation of the Hebrew Bible for Jewish readers.

check.q: Why do new Bible translations keep being made?
check.why: English words shift over time, so translators make new versions that readers today understand.

check.q: One Bible says believeth and another says believes. What is the best explanation?
choices: One is older English, one is newer
One is Hebrew, one is Greek
check.why: Both are English translations of the same Greek verse. The style is old or new, but the meaning is the same.

lessons.title: Synagogue, Church, Home, School
lessons.mainIdea: People read the Bible in different places and for different reasons: worship, family, and study.
reading: In a *synagogue*, Jews read the Torah from a handwritten scroll. It is read in Hebrew, a portion each week, all year long. When the year ends, the readers roll the scroll back to Genesis and start again. Many Jewish families also read at home, at holidays like Passover.

In a *church*, Christians read from both testaments, often out loud during a service. Some churches follow a set list of readings each week. Others let the preacher choose. Many Christians also read at home, alone or with family, and in Sunday classes for children.

In a public *school* like ours, we read the Bible a different way. We study it as literature and history. We ask what a book says, who wrote it, and how Jews and Christians read it. We do not say it is true or false. That is a question for families and houses of worship, not for this class.

words.d: a Jewish house of worship and study, where the Torah is read from a scroll
a Christian house of worship, where the Bible is read aloud in services
a handwritten copy of the first five books, rolled on two wooden rods and read in synagogue

look.title: Reading Aloud, Long Ago
look.text: The book of Nehemiah tells of a day when Ezra the scribe read the Torah aloud to a crowd in Jerusalem, from morning until midday. Helpers stood with him and explained the words, so that everyone there could understand what was read.
look.cite: Nehemiah 8:1–8, paraphrased from the Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917)
look.prompt: Ezra's helpers explained the reading so people understood. How is that like what happens in a synagogue, a church or a classroom today?

check.q: How is the Torah read in a synagogue?
choices: From a scroll, in Hebrew, a portion each week
Only once a year, on Passover
check.why: Synagogues read the Torah from a handwritten scroll, in Hebrew, in weekly portions across the year.

check.q: How does a public school class study the Bible?
choices: As a book everyone must believe
As a book that is proven false
Only by reading the New Testament
check.why: In a public school, the Bible is studied as literature and history, without saying it is true or false.

check.q: In the book of Nehemiah, what did Ezra's helpers do while he read?
choices: Explained the words so people understood
check.why: Nehemiah 8 says the helpers gave the sense of the reading so the crowd could understand.

lessons.title: Bibles in Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois has many kinds of readers, and Chicago once hosted a world meeting where people of many faiths spoke about their scriptures.
reading: Walk through any Chicago neighborhood and you pass synagogues, churches and mosques. Inside, people read scriptures in Hebrew, English, Spanish, Polish, Greek, Arabic and more. Some churches are over a hundred years old. Some meet in storefronts. Each one has its own way of reading.

In 1893, Chicago held a giant fair called the World's Columbian Exposition. As part of it, the city hosted the *World's Parliament of Religions*. Speakers from Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism and other traditions came to talk. Many people in America heard about religions from Asia for the first time.

That meeting showed something this class tries to do. People with different holy books can sit in one room. They can explain what they read and listen to each other. They do not have to agree. You can be a Jewish reader, a Christian reader, a Muslim reader, or not a religious reader at all, and still learn the library together.

words.d: a meeting in Chicago in 1893 where speakers from many religions talked about their traditions
a Muslim house of worship, where the Qur'an is read in Arabic

look.title: One Room, Many Books
look.text: Imagine a long table in a Chicago hall in 1893. On it sit a Torah scroll, a Christian Bible, a Qur'an, and books from India and Japan. The people around the table each hold a different book. Each takes a turn saying what the book means to them.
look.prompt: What rules would you want at that table so that every person could speak and be heard? How could those rules help our class?

check.q: What happened in Chicago in 1893?
choices: The King James Bible was printed
The World's Parliament of Religions met
The first synagogue in America opened
check.why: The World's Parliament of Religions met in Chicago in 1893, during the World's Columbian Exposition.

check.q: Which book is read in Arabic in a mosque?
check.why: Muslims read the Qur'an, and it is recited in Arabic in a mosque.

check.q: What did the 1893 meeting show that this class tries to do?
choices: Let people of different faiths explain and listen
check.why: The Parliament brought many traditions into one room to speak and listen, not to decide who was right.

review.q: The Bible is best described as what?
choices: A single story by one author
review.why: Bible means "the books." It is a collection of many books of different kinds.

review.q: What is the Jewish name for the Hebrew Bible?
review.why: Tanakh comes from Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim, the three parts of the Hebrew Bible.

review.q: How many books are in a Catholic Bible?
review.why: Catholic Bibles have 73 books, including Tobit, Judith and the books of Maccabees.

review.q: In Genesis 1:1, what does the 1 after the colon mean?
review.why: The number after the colon is the verse. Genesis 1:1 is chapter 1, verse 1.

review.q: Which language was the New Testament written in?
review.why: The New Testament was written in Greek, the common language of the Roman world.

review.q: What year was the King James Version finished?
review.why: The King James Version was finished in 1611 after seven years of work.

review.q: Which sentence about chapter numbers is true?
choices: They are in the original scrolls
review.why: Stephen Langton divided the books into chapters in the early 1200s, long after they were written.

review.q: How is the Bible read in this public school class?
choices: As a book that must be believed
As a book that is false
review.why: The class studies what the books say and how Jews and Christians read them, without judging whether they are true.

chapters.title: The Torah's Big Story: Creation to Sinai
chapters.bigQuestion: How do five books tell one long story from the making of the world to the edge of a promised land?

story.title: A Map on Butcher Paper
story.kicker: A class draws the whole journey of the Torah, from Ur to Egypt to the edge of Canaan, on one long sheet.
paragraphs: Mr. Bell rolls a sheet of butcher paper across three desks pushed together. It is longer than a car. "Today we draw the first five books of the Bible," he says. "Not the words. The trip." He hands out markers. "Start on the far right. That is the east. A city called Ur."

Priya draws a little city with a tower. "Genesis says Abraham's family left Ur and went northwest to Haran," Mr. Bell says. "Then the story says God told Abraham to go to a land called Canaan." Priya draws an arrow that curves up and then down along the sea. Next to it, Jonah writes ABRAHAM in big letters.

"Now, Genesis ends with the family going down to Egypt," says Mr. Bell. "Joseph is there first. Then his brothers and their father Jacob come during a famine." Someone draws a pyramid on the far left. Someone else draws a lot of stick people. "That is the whole family. The text says they grew into a people while they lived in Egypt."

Then comes Exodus. The class draws a river, then a sea with a gap in the middle, then a mountain with lightning on top. "That is Sinai," Mr. Bell says. "Exodus says the people got the Ten Commandments there." After that the arrow wanders. It loops. It doubles back. "Numbers says they wandered forty years," he explains. "So draw it long."

At last the arrow reaches a small mountain across from a river. Mr. Bell writes MOUNT NEBO. "Deuteronomy ends here. Moses stands on this mountain and looks at Canaan. The text says he will not cross over." The class looks at the long sheet, city to pyramid to mountain to river. Five books. One trip. "Tomorrow," Mr. Bell says, "we walk it."
story.think: The map goes from Ur to Egypt to the edge of Canaan but never into it. Why do you think the Torah ends right at the edge, before the people go in?

lessons.title: Genesis to Deuteronomy
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah is the first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy, in that order.
reading: The first five books of the Bible go together. Jews call them the *Torah*. Christians often call them the Books of Moses or the *Pentateuch*, a Greek word that means five scrolls. Their names in English are Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. Learn the order. It is the order of the story.

The English names come from Greek and tell what each book is about. Genesis means beginning. Exodus means going out. Leviticus is about the priests, who came from the tribe of Levi. Numbers is named for two counts of the people. Deuteronomy means second law, because Moses repeats the laws.

In Hebrew, each book is named for its first important word. Genesis is Bereshit, "in the beginning." Exodus is Shemot, "names." So the same book can have two names, one Greek and one Hebrew. Both point to the same scroll. Jewish tradition and Christian tradition both say Moses is at the center of these books.

words.d: the first five books of the Bible; the Hebrew word means teaching or instruction
a Greek name for the first five books; it means five scrolls
the first book of the Bible; the name means beginning

look.title: Five Books, Chapter by Chapter
look.cite: Chapter counts as printed in the King James Version (1611) and the JPS Tanakh (1917)
look.prompt: Genesis is the longest of the five. It covers creation, the flood and four generations of one family. Why might a book that covers so much need the most chapters?

check.q: Which is the correct order of the first five books?
check.why: The order is Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy. It follows the story from creation to the edge of Canaan.

check.q: What does the Greek word Pentateuch mean?
check.why: Pentateuch means five scrolls. It is a Christian name for the Torah.

check.q: Why is the book called Exodus?
choices: It is about a count of the people
It is about the beginning of the world
It is about the people going out of Egypt
check.why: Exodus means going out. The book tells how the people left Egypt.

lessons.title: What Torah Means
lessons.mainIdea: Torah means teaching, and Jews read it from a scroll while Christians read it as the start of the Old Testament.
reading: The Hebrew word Torah is often translated as law. But its plain meaning is closer to *teaching* or instruction. The Torah has laws in it. It also has stories, family lists, songs and speeches. All of it, Jewish tradition says, is teaching.

In a synagogue, the Torah is kept as a handwritten *scroll*, rolled on two wooden rods. A trained writer copies every letter by hand. Each week a portion is read aloud in Hebrew. Over one year, the readers go from Genesis to the end of Deuteronomy. Then they roll it back and begin again on a holiday called Simchat Torah.

Christians read these same five books as the first part of the Old Testament. They read them from a printed Bible, in their own language. Jews and Christians both believe these books matter. They often read them differently, and we will notice those differences as we go.

words.d: the plain meaning of the word Torah; instruction, not only law
a long roll of parchment; the Torah is read from a scroll in synagogue
a Jewish holiday when the yearly Torah reading ends and starts over at Genesis

look.title: Law or Teaching?
look.text: Two students look at the word Torah. One says, "It means law, so the Torah is a rulebook." The other says, "It means teaching, so the stories about Abraham and Joseph are Torah too, not just the rules."
look.prompt: Which student's idea fits better with a book that has stories, songs and speeches as well as rules? Explain your answer.

check.q: What is the plain meaning of the Hebrew word Torah?
check.why: Torah means teaching or instruction. It includes laws, stories and more.

check.q: How is the Torah kept in a synagogue?
choices: As a handwritten scroll on wooden rods
check.why: Synagogues keep the Torah as a scroll, copied by hand and read aloud in portions.

check.q: What happens on Simchat Torah?
choices: The yearly reading ends and starts over
The scroll is put away for a year
check.why: On Simchat Torah, the last portion of Deuteronomy is read and the scroll is rolled back to Genesis.

lessons.title: Creation and a Garden
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis opens with the story of God making the world in six days and resting on the seventh, then a garden where a rule is broken.
reading: Genesis begins with the words "In the beginning." The story says God made light on the first day. Then sky, then land and sea and plants, then sun, moon and stars. Then fish and birds. Then animals and people. On the seventh day, the text says, God rested. Jews keep the *Sabbath*, a day of rest, and connect it to this story.

Chapter 2 tells of a garden called *Eden*. The story says God put the first man there and made a woman from his side. They could eat from every tree but one. A snake told the woman the fruit was good to eat. She ate, and so did the man. The story says they had to leave the garden.

Jews and Christians read this story in different ways. Many Christians call the broken rule the fall and connect it to why people sin. Jewish tradition usually does not read it that way. It sees the story more as the start of human choice. Both agree the story is about people, a rule, and a choice.

words.d: a weekly day of rest; Genesis connects it to God resting on the seventh day
the garden in Genesis 2 and 3 where the story places the first people

look.title: The First Words Spoken
look.text: And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.
look.prompt: In this verse, how does the story say God makes light? What does this tell you about the way Genesis 1 pictures creation?

check.q: According to Genesis 1, what did God do on the seventh day?
check.why: Genesis 1 and 2 say God rested on the seventh day. Jews connect the Sabbath to this.

check.q: What is Eden?
check.why: Eden is the garden in Genesis 2 and 3 where the first people lived.

check.q: How do Jewish and Christian readers often differ on the Eden story?
choices: Many Christians call it the fall; Jewish tradition usually does not
Jews say there was no snake
Christians say there was no garden
They read it exactly the same way
check.why: Many Christians read the story as the fall. Jewish tradition more often reads it as the start of human choice.

lessons.title: The Flood and the Tower
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis tells of a great flood, a rainbow promise, and a tower where languages were mixed.
reading: Genesis 6 says the world had filled with violence. The story says God chose one man, Noah, to build a huge boat called an *ark*. Noah brought his family and animals of every kind inside. Rain fell for forty days. Everything outside the ark was covered. At last the water went down and the ark rested on a mountain.

After the flood, the text says God set a rainbow in the clouds. It was a sign of a *covenant*, a binding promise, that a flood would never again destroy the earth. This is the first of several covenants in the Torah. Each one is a promise between God and people, and this one is with every living thing.

Genesis 11 tells of a tower in a city called Babel. The story says people wanted to build it up to the sky. God mixed up their language so they could not understand each other, and they spread across the earth. The story explains, in its own way, why people speak so many languages.

words.d: the huge boat Noah builds in Genesis 6 to 8
a binding promise; in the Hebrew Bible, a bond between God and people
the city in Genesis 11 where the story says languages were mixed at a tower

look.title: The Sign in the Clouds
look.text: I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth.
look.prompt: The word bow here means rainbow, and token means sign. Who is the covenant between? Why might a rainbow be a good sign for a promise about rain?

check.q: What is the ark in the story of Noah?
check.why: The ark is the boat Noah builds to hold his family and the animals.

check.q: What does the rainbow stand for in Genesis 9?
choices: A covenant that a flood will not destroy the earth again
A sign that the tower would fall
A map to the promised land
check.why: Genesis 9 says the rainbow is the sign of a covenant that the earth will not be flooded again.

check.q: What does the story of Babel explain?
choices: Why people rest on the Sabbath
check.why: Genesis 11 tells how languages were mixed at Babel and people spread across the earth.

lessons.title: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis tells of one family, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who received a promise of land and many descendants.
reading: In Genesis 12, the story turns to one man, *Abraham*. The text says God told him to leave his home and go to a land he would be shown. God promised to make him a great nation. Abraham and his wife Sarah went to Canaan. They were old and had no children, but the story says they trusted the promise.

A son, *Isaac*, was born when they were very old. Isaac married Rebekah. They had twin sons, Esau and Jacob, who fought over their father's blessing. Jacob had to run away. One night he dreamed of a ladder to heaven with angels going up and down. Later the text says he wrestled a stranger and got a new name, Israel.

Jacob had twelve sons. Their families became the twelve tribes of *Israel*. Jews call Abraham, Isaac and Jacob the patriarchs, the fathers. They call Sarah, Rebekah, Leah and Rachel the matriarchs, the mothers. Christians and Muslims also honor Abraham. All three traditions tell his story in their own way.

words.d: the man in Genesis 12 whom the story says God called to go to Canaan with a promise
the son of Abraham and Sarah, born when they were very old
the new name given to Jacob; also the name of the people who came from his twelve sons

look.title: The Promise to Abraham
look.text: And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing:
look.prompt: Thee and thy mean you and your. What three things does the text say God promises Abraham here? Which promise would take the longest to come true?

check.q: Where did the story say Abraham and Sarah went?
check.why: Genesis 12 says Abraham left his home and traveled to Canaan.

check.q: Who were Isaac's twin sons?
check.why: Isaac and Rebekah had twins, Esau and Jacob. Jacob later got the name Israel.

check.q: What does Jewish tradition call Abraham, Isaac and Jacob?
check.why: The patriarchs are the fathers of the people of Israel. The matriarchs are the mothers.

lessons.title: Joseph in Egypt
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis ends with Joseph, sold by his brothers, rising in Egypt and bringing his whole family there.
reading: Jacob loved his son *Joseph* best and gave him a fine coat. Joseph told his brothers about dreams where they bowed to him. The brothers grew angry. The story says they sold him to traders, who took him to *Egypt*. They told their father he was dead.

In Egypt, Joseph was a slave, then a prisoner. But the text says he could explain dreams. Pharaoh, the king, dreamed of seven fat cows and seven thin cows. Joseph said it meant seven good years and then seven years of famine. Pharaoh put Joseph in charge of storing food.

When the famine came, Joseph's brothers went to Egypt to buy grain. They did not know the man in charge was Joseph. He tested them, then wept and told them who he was. He forgave them. The whole family, with old Jacob, moved to Egypt. That is how Genesis ends, with the family safe but far from Canaan.

words.d: Jacob's son, sold by his brothers, who rose to power in Egypt
the land of the Nile where Joseph's family settled and, Exodus says, later became slaves
a long time when there is not enough food

look.title: The Man in Charge
look.text: Ten brothers stand before an Egyptian official to buy grain. He wears Egyptian clothes and speaks through an interpreter. They do not know him. He knows every one of them. Years ago, they sold him to traders and lied to their father.
look.prompt: What choices does Joseph have at this moment? Genesis says he forgives them in the end. Why might the story make forgiving so hard and slow?

check.q: What did Joseph's brothers do to him?
choices: Sold him to traders going to Egypt
check.why: Genesis 37 says the brothers sold Joseph, and he was taken to Egypt.

check.q: What did Pharaoh's dream of fat and thin cows mean, according to Joseph?
choices: Seven good years, then seven years of famine
check.why: Joseph said the dream meant seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine.

check.q: How does the book of Genesis end?
choices: With the people at Mount Sinai
With Jacob's family living in Egypt
check.why: Genesis ends with Jacob's whole family settled in Egypt under Joseph's care.

lessons.title: Moses and the Plagues
lessons.mainIdea: Exodus says the family became a people, was enslaved, and Moses was sent to tell Pharaoh to let them go.
reading: Exodus opens many years after Joseph. The family has grown into a people, the Israelites. A new *Pharaoh* fears them and makes them *slaves*. He even orders baby boys killed. One mother hides her baby in a basket on the Nile. Pharaoh's daughter finds him and names him Moses.

Moses grows up in the palace, but runs away after killing a man who beat a slave. In the desert, the text says, he sees a bush on fire that does not burn up. A voice tells him to go back and lead the people out. Moses says he is not a good speaker. His brother Aaron goes with him.

Moses tells Pharaoh, "Let my people go." Pharaoh says no. The story says ten *plagues* strike Egypt: the river turns to blood, frogs, gnats, flies, sick animals, boils, hail, locusts, darkness, and last, the death of the firstborn. Only after the tenth does Pharaoh let them leave.

words.d: the king of Egypt
a person owned by another and forced to work; Exodus says the Israelites were slaves in Egypt
one of ten disasters that Exodus says struck Egypt before Pharaoh let the people go

look.title: At the Burning Bush
look.text: And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
look.prompt: Moses asks what name to give the people. What answer does the text give? Why do you think this answer has puzzled and interested readers for so long?

check.q: Why did the new Pharaoh make the Israelites slaves?
choices: He feared them because they had grown so many
check.why: Exodus 1 says the new king feared the Israelites because they had grown into a large people.

check.q: Where did Moses hear the voice telling him to go back to Egypt?
check.why: Exodus 3 tells of a bush on fire that did not burn up, where Moses was told to lead the people out.

check.q: How many plagues does Exodus describe?
check.why: Exodus 7 to 12 tell of ten plagues, ending with the death of the firstborn.

lessons.title: Passover and the Sea
lessons.mainIdea: Exodus tells of the night of Passover and the crossing of the sea, which Jews remember every year.
reading: Before the last plague, the text says each family was told to roast a lamb and mark their doorposts with its blood. Death would pass over those houses. They ate in a hurry, with bread that had no time to rise. This night is called *Passover*. Jews still remember it every spring with a special meal called a seder.

The Israelites left Egypt that night. But Pharaoh changed his mind and chased them with chariots. They came to a sea with no way across. The story says Moses lifted his hand and the water split. The people walked through on dry ground. When the Egyptians followed, the water came back.

Exodus 15 has a song the people sang on the far shore. Miriam, Moses's sister, led the women with a drum. Jews read this story as the birth of their people. Christians read it too, and many connect it to Easter, which often falls near Passover. Muslims also tell of Moses and the sea in the Qur'an.

words.d: the Jewish holiday that remembers the night the Israelites left Egypt
the Passover meal where the story of leaving Egypt is retold
the sister of Moses who led the women in song after the sea crossing

look.title: Numbers in the Exodus Story
rows: Days of rain in the flood
look.cite: Genesis 7, Exodus 7–12, Exodus 20 and Numbers 14, King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: The numbers 40, 12 and 10 come up again and again in these books. Why might a story use the same numbers over and over?

check.q: What is the seder?
choices: The Passover meal where the story is retold
The mountain where the law was given
check.why: The seder is the Passover meal. Families retell the story of leaving Egypt during it.

check.q: Why is the holiday called Passover?
choices: The people passed over the sea
The people passed over the mountain
Death passed over the marked houses
check.why: Exodus 12 says death passed over the houses marked with the lamb's blood.

check.q: Who led the women in song after the crossing of the sea?
check.why: Exodus 15 says Miriam took a drum and led the women in a song.

lessons.title: Sinai and the Ten Commandments
lessons.mainIdea: At Mount Sinai, Exodus says, God gave the people the Ten Commandments and made a covenant with them.
reading: Three months after leaving Egypt, the people camped at *Mount Sinai*. The text says the mountain shook with thunder, smoke and a trumpet sound. Moses went up. The story says God spoke ten sayings, which most people call the *Ten Commandments*. Later the text says they were written on two stone tablets.

In plain words, the commandments say this. Worship only God. Make no idols. Do not misuse God's name. Keep the Sabbath. Honor your parents. Do not murder. Do not cheat on your husband or wife. Do not steal. Do not lie about others. Do not want what is not yours. Jews, Catholics and Protestants number them a little differently. The words are the same.

At Sinai the people agreed to keep these and many other laws. This agreement is a covenant. Exodus says God promised to be with them. They promised to obey. Jews call this the covenant at Sinai. They keep the holiday of Shavuot to remember it. Christians read these laws too. Most say the Ten Commandments still guide them.

words.d: the mountain where Exodus says the Ten Commandments were given
the ten sayings in Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5, from worship only God to do not want what is not yours
a Jewish holiday that remembers the giving of the Torah at Sinai

look.title: Two of the Ten
look.text: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. ... Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
look.prompt: One of these two commandments is about time and one is about family. Which one gives a reason for keeping it? What is the reason?

check.q: Where does Exodus say the Ten Commandments were given?
check.why: Exodus 19 and 20 place the giving of the commandments at Mount Sinai.

check.q: Which of these is one of the Ten Commandments?
check.why: Do not steal is one of the ten. The others are events from stories, not commandments.

check.q: Which holiday do Jews keep to remember the Torah given at Sinai?
check.why: Shavuot remembers the giving of the Torah at Sinai. Passover remembers leaving Egypt.

sections.title: The Long Road and the Covenant

lessons.title: Years in the Wilderness
lessons.mainIdea: Leviticus gives laws for worship and daily life, and Numbers tells of forty years of wandering in the desert.
reading: Leviticus is the book in the middle. It has few stories. Instead it gives laws for the priests and the people: how to offer sacrifices, which animals may be eaten, how to treat neighbors and strangers. One famous line says to love your neighbor as yourself. Jewish tradition has studied these laws for thousands of years.

Numbers begins with a count of the people, which is how it got its name. Then the people march toward Canaan. The text says they sent twelve *spies* ahead. Ten came back afraid of the people living there. The Israelites refused to go in. The story says that because of this, they had to wander forty years in the *wilderness*.

During those years, the text says, food called *manna* appeared on the ground each morning. Water came from a rock. The people complained often. Moses grew tired. Numbers is a book about a long, hard wait. It ends with a new generation camped across the river from Canaan, ready at last.

words.d: the twelve men Numbers says were sent ahead to look at Canaan
the desert between Egypt and Canaan where the people wandered forty years
the food that Exodus and Numbers say appeared each morning in the wilderness

look.title: Ten Say No, Two Say Go
look.text: Twelve men return from Canaan. Ten say, "The cities are strong and the people are giants. We cannot do it." Two, Joshua and Caleb, say, "The land is good. We can go." The crowd listens to the ten and weeps all night.
look.prompt: Why do you think the crowd believed the ten and not the two? What does the story seem to say about fear and trust?

check.q: What is Leviticus mostly about?
choices: Laws for worship and daily life
check.why: Leviticus is mostly laws for priests and people, including how to treat neighbors and strangers.

check.q: How did the book of Numbers get its name?
check.why: Numbers begins and ends with a count of the people.

check.q: Why does Numbers say the people wandered forty years?
choices: They were afraid to enter Canaan after the spies' report
Moses wanted to build a city
check.why: Numbers 13 and 14 say the people refused to enter Canaan out of fear, and so they wandered.

lessons.title: Moses Looks at the Land
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy is Moses's farewell; he repeats the law, and the Torah ends with him seeing Canaan but not entering.
reading: Deuteronomy is made of speeches. Moses stands before the new generation and tells the whole story again: Egypt, the sea, Sinai, the wilderness. He repeats the Ten Commandments. He gives the *Shema*, the words "Hear, O Israel," which Jews say every day. He tells the people to love God with all their heart.

Then Moses climbs *Mount Nebo*. The text says God showed him the whole land of Canaan from the top. But Moses would not go in. He died on the mountain, the story says, and no one knows where he is buried. Joshua would lead the people across the river. The Torah ends there, at the edge.

The Torah's big story is held together by *covenant*, a promise with rules on both sides. God promises land, family and care; the people promise to keep the law. Jews read these five books every year as the heart of their Bible. Christians read them as the start of the story they believe continues in Jesus. Both keep reading them, together and apart.

words.d: the words "Hear, O Israel" in Deuteronomy 6, which Jews say in daily prayer
the mountain where Deuteronomy says Moses saw the land and died
a binding promise with rules on both sides; the bond between God and Israel in the Torah

look.title: Hear, O Israel
look.text: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD: And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.
look.prompt: Jews say these words morning and evening. Christians know them because the Gospels say Jesus quoted them. What does the verse ask a person to do, and with how much of themselves?

check.q: What is Deuteronomy mostly made of?
check.why: Deuteronomy is Moses's farewell speeches, retelling the story and repeating the law.

check.q: What happens to Moses at the end of the Torah?
choices: He leads the people into Canaan
He sees Canaan from Mount Nebo but does not enter
check.why: Deuteronomy 34 says Moses saw the land from Mount Nebo and died there. Joshua led the people across.

check.q: What is a covenant, as this chapter uses the word?
choices: A promise with rules on both sides
check.why: A covenant is a binding promise. In the Torah, God promises land and care, and the people promise to keep the law.

review.q: What does the word Torah mean in plain Hebrew?
review.why: Torah means teaching or instruction. Pentateuch is the Greek name meaning five scrolls.

review.q: Which book tells of the flood, Abraham and Joseph?
review.why: All of these stories are in Genesis, the first book.

review.q: What is the sign of the covenant after the flood?
review.why: Genesis 9 says the rainbow is the sign that a flood will not destroy the earth again.

review.q: Which book tells of the plagues, Passover and Mount Sinai?
review.why: Exodus tells how the people left Egypt and received the law at Sinai.

review.q: Why did the people wander forty years, according to Numbers?
choices: Pharaoh would not let them leave
They were afraid to enter Canaan
review.why: Numbers 13 and 14 say the people refused to go in after the spies' report.

choices: The words "Hear, O Israel" that Jews say daily
review.why: The Shema is Deuteronomy 6:4, "Hear, O Israel," said in Jewish daily prayer.

choices: At the edge of Canaan, with Moses on Mount Nebo
review.why: Deuteronomy 34 ends with Moses seeing Canaan from Mount Nebo. The people have not yet crossed.

choices: A binding promise with rules on both sides
review.why: A covenant is a binding promise. In the Torah it is the bond between God and Israel.
